narrative:
The model predicted a 63% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile is far below the average of students who were accepted, signaling that your later-year performance raised serious concerns about readiness for the bar. Your first-year class ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure; again, a bottom-decile placement is well below the typical accepted student.

Your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction. At 30.5 it is lower than the 37.2 average of accepted students, yet the model still treated this score as a modest positive signal that slightly increased the chance you might pass. Unfortunately, this helpful nudge was not large enough to overcome the negative impact of your class rankings.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.20, family income bracket, gender, race, and plan to attend full-time played little or no role in the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s. Stronger grades and a higher test score in a future application would directly address the factors that led to this rejection.
